description: Please sketch a modern cylinder vacuum cleaner—featuring a rounded, compact body with prominent rear wheels, a top handle, an integrated controls panel, a flexible hose connection, and a telescopic wand leading to a floor head—from two different viewpoints. For each viewpoint, provide two distinct versions: a 'concept view' that retains all your initial perspective scaffolding, center axes, bounding boxes, intersecting ellipses, and internal cross-sectional lines, and a polished 'presentation view' that uses clean, confident contour lines with all underlying construction hidden. You should deliver a total of four sketches that clearly show your underlying structural thinking right next to the final, clean presentation.
creativity_reasoning: The design demonstrates a clean and contemporary form language with a compact, rounded body that aligns with modern consumer products. However, it lacks inventive features or novel reinterpretations of the vacuum cleaner form, staying within the bounds of conventional design.
originality_reasoning: The design closely resembles existing commercial cylinder vacuums, with no distinctive visual or functional elements that set it apart. The sketches show good industrial design restraint but do not introduce a unique signature element.
usefulness_relevance_reasoning: The design effectively demonstrates technical illustration workflow and addresses some key elements of the brief, such as compact body and wheel placement. However, it falls short in representing the full product scenario, as several functional components like the handle and hose system are missing.
clarity_reasoning: The side-by-side concept and presentation views clearly communicate the structural thinking and final form, with consistent perspective and volume. However, clarity is reduced where functional features are implied rather than explicitly drawn.
level_of_detail_elaboration_reasoning: The sketches include robust construction lines and bounding boxes, transitioning well into clean presentation views. However, the design remains at a primary form stage, lacking detailed product-specific elements and a complete vacuum system representation.
feasibility_reasoning: The design is technically and economically viable, with manufacturable geometry and standard components. Feasibility could be enhanced with clearer packaging cues and more explicit functional interfaces, but nothing suggests an impossible build.
instructor_feedback_intro: You're hitting the 'construction sweet spot'! Your work shows a strong grasp of perspective scaffolding and clean linework, effectively translating structural thinking into polished product forms.
instructor_feedback_pivot: Focus on fully integrating the complete vacuum system into your design. Ensure that key components like the handle, controls, and hose system are clearly represented to avoid the design feeling incomplete.
instructor_feedback_next_step: Add a focused feature pass to one viewpoint: draw the hose port with swivel/locking detail, a clearly placed handle, and a simple control UI. Include a quick side sketch of the wand and floor head to ensure the product reads as a complete, usable vacuum system.

persona.name: Clara Davidson
persona.title: Industrial Design Sketching Professor
persona.prompt: You are an expert design critic and creativity researcher. Your task is to evaluate a design concept consisting of a sketch and a text description. As an Industrial Design Sketching Professor, you will focus specifically on the clarity of perspective and the effectiveness of structural representation in the sketches.

result.creativity_reasoning: The form language shows thoughtful exploration of a compact, rounded cylinder-vac body with a clear “soft monolith” vibe and a few nice surfacing moves (the wrapped top panel and the recessed front feature). However, the concept stays within a fairly standard canister-vac typology and doesn’t introduce a notably new interaction, storage, or modularity idea beyond the refined casing.
result.originality_reasoning: The overall silhouette and component layout (rear wheels, top handle zone, front hose port) reads as familiar and close to existing consumer vacuums. The sketching focuses more on clean industrial surfacing than on a distinct new architecture, so the uniqueness is modest.
result.usefulness_relevance_reasoning: The design addresses the prompt’s key elements well: compact body, prominent rear wheels, top handle area, a front connection point, and two viewpoints with both construction and presentation versions. The object reads as a vacuum cleaner immediately, and the wheel placement suggests practical roll stability and maneuverability.
result.clarity_reasoning: Your presentation views communicate the main massing clearly, and the concept views show solid intent with bounding boxes, centerlines, and ellipses. Clarity drops because some perspective cues are inconsistent between features: wheel ellipses don’t always share the same minor-axis orientation as the body’s perspective, and a few surface seams/contours don’t fully wrap in a way that confirms the underlying 3D turn. Also, the hose/wand/floor head system requested in the description is not clearly depicted, so the full product system is only partially communicated.
result.level_of_detail_elaboration_reasoning: You provide four sketches (two viewpoints × concept/presentation), and the construction layers are present and useful. Detail is still mid-level: controls panel, handle definition, hose connection geometry, and functional part breaks (lid, bin access, cord management) are implied rather than explicitly designed. The wand and floor head are largely absent, which reduces completeness relative to the brief.
result.feasibility_reasoning: The casing volumes, wheel integration, and general parting logic look manufacturable with typical injection-molded shells and simple wheel hubs. The surfacing is smooth and plausible. Feasibility would be stronger if you clarified where the handle structurally anchors, how the hose port seals/locks, and where service access/emptying occurs, but nothing shown appears technically unrealistic.
result.instructor_feedback:
You’re building a strong “scaffold-to-surface” workflow! The big win here is that your concept views genuinely show structural thinking—bounding boxes, center axes, and ellipse families—and your presentation views simplify into confident primary forms with readable highlights and shadow direction. The vacuum’s massing feels stable and compact, and the rear wheel emphasis is clear. Where the drawings need more discipline is perspective consistency: the wheel ellipses, front port ellipse, and the body’s cross-contours aren’t always agreeing on the same vanishing logic, which slightly flattens the volume. Also, the brief asks for the full cleaning system (hose → telescopic wand → floor head), and right now the sketches read mostly as the canister body without the complete functional chain.

Where we need to pivot: lock your ellipse alignment to one perspective system per view (shared minor axes, consistent degree changes along the length), and use 2–3 deliberate wraparound cross-contours to “prove” the curvature transitions. Avoid adding extra construction lines that don’t resolve into a clear plane change—keep scaffolding purposeful so it supports, rather than muddies, the read. Finally, don’t leave the accessory system implicit: the hose connection needs a clear interface (collar, latch, swivel), and the wand/head should be drawn as secondary forms to communicate usability and scale.

Your Next Step: do one additional page per viewpoint with (1) a clean 2-point perspective box, (2) a single centerline down the body, (3) three matched ellipse sets (wheel, port, body cross-section) that all share the same perspective logic, then (4) add the hose + telescopic wand + floor head as simple cylinders/boxes first, before refining. After that, re-ink one presentation view using line-weight hierarchy (thicker silhouette, thinner internal seams) to make the form read instantly.
